0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
See how you translated the term **Sheminith** in the superscription to Psalm 6.

1.note: See how you translated the phrase **the godly** in 4:3. Alternate translation: [godly people]

The psalmist is using **the sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “all human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the human race] or [from humanity]

2.note: The psalmist is not referring to a specific **Man**. He means all wicked people among mankind in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Mankind speaks with falsehood with their neighbors]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [lies] or [what is untrue]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if anyone a person speaks to were actually their **neighbor**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [other people]

These two phrases, **with lip of smoothness** and **with a heart and a heart**, mean very similar things. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating a similar idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with deceptive flattery]

The psalmist is using **lip of smoothness** as a common expression of his culture to mean “flattering speech.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with flattering words]

The psalmist is using **with a heart and a heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “with divided loyalty” or “with deceitful intentions.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with deceitful hearts] or [speaking dishonestly]

3.note: The psalmist is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy” or “bring to an end.” See how you translated the expression “with lip of smoothness” in the previous verse. So in this context, **cut off all lips of smoothness** means “bring to an end all those who speak with flattering lips.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh bring to an end all people who speak with flattering words] or [May Yahweh stop all people who speak with flattering speech]

Here, **tongue** represents a person who speaks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the person speaking great things]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh cut off the tongue speaking great things]

The implication is that the people who are **speaking great things** are bragging and making proud claims. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that brags] or [that makes proud claims]

4.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [lips which say]

Here, **tongue** and **lips** represent speech and the ability to speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [We will prevail through what we say. We can speak as we please]

Here the wicked people are speaking of their **tongue** as if it were a weapon that could defeat others. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By our speech we will defeat others] or [We will overpower others with our words]

The implication is that these speakers are claiming to be in complete control of what they say and do not need to answer to anyone else. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [We can say whatever we want]

The speakers are using the question **who is master over us?** as a way of making a defiant statement. They are not expecting an answer but are expressing their belief that no one has authority over them. If a speaker of your language would not use a question form for this purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one will be master over us!]

5.note: These two phrases **Because of oppression of the poor** and **because of the groaning of the needy** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation, if possible. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Because of how the poor are being cruelly oppressed and suffering]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [poor people … of needy people]

Here, **groaning** represents the suffering of the needy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because the needy are suffering so severely that it causes them to groan] or [because of the suffering of the needy]

Yahweh is using **Now I will arise** as a common expression of the culture to indicate that he is about to take action against those who oppress the poor and needy. He is not saying that he will get out of bed or stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I will take action]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **safety**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will keep safe]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if someone were actually **panting** for safety like a thirsty person pants for water. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he longs for it]

It might seem that the expression **he pants for** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [he pants for] or [he longs for]

6.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh’s **pure words** were actually refined **silver**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [are pure words, like silver]

6.q: כֶּ֣סֶף צָ֭רוּף בַּ⁠עֲלִ֣יל לָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ מְ֝זֻקָּ֗ק שִׁבְעָתָֽיִם
6.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s promises were actually **silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven** times. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [like silver that is refined in a furnace on the ground seven times]

6.q: כֶּ֣סֶף צָ֭רוּף בַּ⁠עֲלִ֣יל לָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ מְ֝זֻקָּ֗ק שִׁבְעָתָֽיִם
6.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [silver that is refined in a furnace on the ground seven times] or [pure like silver that is refined seven time in a furnace on the ground]

7.note: David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will keep them** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is Yahweh himself who will **keep** and **protect** “the poor” and “the needy” mentioned in verse 5. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Indeed, it is you Yahweh who will keep them]

These two phrases **you will keep them** and **You will protect him** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [You yourself, Yahweh, will surely keep the poor and the needy safe]

The pronoun **them** refers to the poor and needy people, while the pronoun **him** also refers to these same people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You yourself Yahweh will keep the poor and needy. You will protect the poor and the needy]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that the phrase **for eternity** means “forever” or “continually.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [forever]

8.q: סָבִ֗יב רְשָׁעִ֥ים יִתְהַלָּכ֑וּ⁠ן כְּ⁠רֻ֥ם זֻ֝לּ֗וּת לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י אָדָֽם
8.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that **The wicked walk about on every side** describes. Alternate translation: [When vileness is exalted among the sons of man, the wicked ones walk about on every side]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in 1:1. Alternate translation: [The wicked people]

By **walk about**, the psalmist means that the wicked walk around freely doing evil things without anyone stopping them and that they walk around proudly as a result of being able to do evil things. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [walk about freely] or [walk about proudly]

The implication is that wicked people are the ones who are promoting or honoring vileness. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [when people exalt vileness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vileness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when what is vile is exalted]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings” or “people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among people] or [among humanity]
